bind Prolific + Sona

final_data = rbind(prolific_data, sona_data)

basic descriptives

final_data %>% pull(subject) %>% unique()
##  [1] 77973    NA 81241 24944 83288 62209 23632 70601 60261 82820 86063 39957
## [13] 94723 93323 36136 93281 24856 93417  7333 84410 35745 44899 36339 28566
## [25]  5637 87962 48052 86307  8328 64524 86113   781 15911 25870 15923 52894
## [37] 26699 83953 75762  7440 38548 87707 54791 49182  5372  1798 25370 40717
## [49] 70075 14467 71296 99038 99802 94288  3888 68576 71373
## 56 total participants 
##(R counted 'NA' as a 57th participant because subject ID apparently was not recorded for the 4 'practice feedback' trials and the 'end screen' trial)

final_data %>% group_by(subject) %>% count()
## R counts 219 (Prolific) or 220 (Sona) trials per subject, but lists 265 trials for subject "NA". This comes from the same experiment coding mistake that I already discovered and explained above. Given the data tagging error mentioned above, we would expect R to undercount the trials per subject by 5 per subject, causing R to count 5x56=280 trials for "NA". The actual number is 273. Upon further inspection, the subject data tag was included for the "end screen" var in the sona code, just not for the prolific code (though the 'feedback' trials were still labeled subject "NA")...:

sona_data %>% pull(subject) %>% unique()
## [1] 71296    NA 99038 99802 94288  3888 68576 71373
## There are 7 sona subjects (excluding "NA"), meaning R should actually be counting (5x56 - 7x1)=273 trials for "subject" NA. This matches the actual count, so we can conclude: 

##Prolific and Sona both have 224 trials per subject.

exclusions

##exclude filler, practice, and non-picture trials
important_data <- final_data %>% filter(typeoftrial=="picture" & !(trialcondition %in% c("filler", "practice")))

##calculate subject accuracy
important_data <- important_data %>% mutate(accuracy=ifelse(correct=="TRUE",1,0))
subject_accuracy <- important_data %>% group_by(subject) %>% summarise(TaskAccuracy=mean(accuracy))

##exclude incorrect responses
data1_CorrectResponse <- important_data %>% filter(accuracy==1) 

##exclude subjects with accuracy > 60%
InaccurateSubjects <- subject_accuracy %>% filter(TaskAccuracy < 0.6)
data2_CorrectResponse_Accuracy <- data1_CorrectResponse %>% filter(!subject %in% InaccurateSubjects)

##total participants after exclusion: 55 (1 excluded--33% accuracy)
data2_CorrectResponse_Accuracy %>% pull(subject) %>% unique()
##  [1] 77973 81241 24944 83288 62209 23632 70601 60261 82820 86063 39957 94723
## [13] 93323 36136 93281 24856 93417  7333 84410 35745 44899 36339 28566  5637
## [25] 87962 48052 86307  8328 64524 86113   781 15911 25870 15923 52894 26699
## [37] 83953 75762  7440 38548 87707 54791 49182  1798 25370 40717 70075 14467
## [49] 71296 99038 99802 94288  3888 68576 71373

transforming RT

##make rt numeric
data2_CorrectResponse_Accuracy <- data2_CorrectResponse_Accuracy %>% mutate(rt = as.numeric(rt))

## rt histogram ----does NOT look normally distributed (positive skew)
data2_CorrectResponse_Accuracy %>% filter(rt <10000) %>% ggplot(aes(x=rt)) + geom_histogram(binwidth =20, fill="pink" ) + theme_economist() + labs(x="RT (ms)", y="frequency", title= "RT histogram")

##rt log (base 10) transformation
data2_CorrectResponse_Accuracy <- data2_CorrectResponse_Accuracy %>% mutate(log10_rt=log(rt, 10))

##log10(rt) histogram
data2_CorrectResponse_Accuracy %>% ggplot(aes(x=log10_rt)) + geom_histogram(binwidth =0.1, fill="pink" ) + theme_economist() + labs(x="log10(rt)", y="frequency", title= "RT histogram")

##looks fairly normal now

compute mean RTs

##Here are each subjects' means for all 4 conditions, and then the overall means for each condition...

subjectMeans<- data2_CorrectResponse_Accuracy %>% group_by(subject, trialcondition) %>% summarise(subj_mean=mean(log10_rt))
## `summarise()` has grouped output by 'subject'. You can override using the
## `.groups` argument.
conditionMeans <- data2_CorrectResponse_Accuracy %>% group_by(trialcondition) %>% summarise(conditionMean=mean(log10_rt))

check assumptions

identify and remove outliers

outliers <- subjectMeans %>% group_by(trialcondition) %>% identify_outliers(subj_mean)
outlier_exclusion <- outliers %>% filter(is.extreme=="TRUE")

subjectMeans2 <- subjectMeans %>% filter(!subject %in% outlier_exclusion)

##2 outliers, no extreme outliers, no exclusions

check normality

##shapiro test
subjectMeans2 %>% group_by(trialcondition) %>% shapiro_test(subj_mean)
##all have p>0.05, but Unsquash-Smashed condition is close at p=0.0852. Data satisfies normality condition

##qqplot....plots look fine, not perfect for unsquashables
subjectMeans2_split <- subjectMeans2 %>% separate(trialcondition, into=c("squashability","state"), sep="_")
ggqqplot(subjectMeans2_split, "subj_mean", ggtheme = theme_bw()) + facet_grid(squashability ~ state, labeller = "label_both")

conduct repeated-measures anova

subjectMeans2_split <- subjectMeans2_split %>% ungroup() 

RManova <- anova_test(data = subjectMeans2_split, dv=subj_mean, wid = subject, within = c(squashability, state), effect.size = "pes")
get_anova_table(RManova)
##no significant main effect for squashability
##significant main effect for state, significant interaction
##no sphericity violation

conduct post-hoc tests (if needed)

##decomposing significant interaction
subjectMeans2_split %>% group_by(squashability) %>% anova_test(dv=subj_mean, wid = subject, within = state, effect.size = "pes") %>% get_anova_table() %>% adjust_pvalue(method = "bonferroni")
#### squashable: p.adj = 1.000
#### unsquashable: p.adj = 0.006 *, partial eta-squared=0.151 (large effect)


#### The RT for the unsquashable objects was significantly different depending on the state of the target object (smashed vs normal), but there was no significant difference found for squashable objects when comparing thee reaction times for normal vs smashed targets. This pattern in the the graph below shows that RTs for unsquashable objects were significantly slower when the target object was smashed compared to when they were normal. This suggests that the participants activated the normal but not the smashed state for the target object when primed by the sentence, despite the fact that a bowling ball was being dropped on it, causing a slower RT than when the normal object was shown. For the squashable objects, the data interpreted in line with the Horachak & Garrido study suggests that both the smashed and unsmashed sates were activated when primed by the bowling ball sentences, resulting in no difference between reaction times when a smashed vs normal image of thw squashable object was shown.

visualize log and raw RT pattern

##condition means for logRT and RT data

subjectMeansRawRT<- data2_CorrectResponse_Accuracy %>% group_by(subject, trialcondition) %>% summarise(subj_meanRaw=mean(rt))
## `summarise()` has grouped output by 'subject'. You can override using the
## `.groups` argument.
subjectMeansRawRT2 <- subjectMeansRawRT %>% filter(!subject %in% outlier_exclusion)

conditionMeansRaw <- subjectMeansRawRT2 %>% group_by(trialcondition) %>% summarise(rawRTmean=mean(subj_meanRaw), sd=sd(subj_meanRaw))

conditionMeansLOG <- subjectMeans2_split %>% group_by(state, squashability) %>% summarise(LogRTmean=mean(subj_mean), sd=sd(subj_mean))
## `summarise()` has grouped output by 'state'. You can override using the
## `.groups` argument.
##sd and SEM calculations

n= subjectMeans2 %>% group_by(subject) %>% n_groups() 

conditionMeansRaw <- conditionMeansRaw %>% mutate(SEM=sd/sqrt(n))
conditionMeansLOG <- conditionMeansLOG %>% mutate(SEM=sd/sqrt(n))

conditionMeansRaw
conditionMeansLOG
##graphs

conditionMeansRaw %>% separate(trialcondition, into = c("squashability","state"), sep="_") %>% ggplot(aes(x=squashability, y=rawRTmean, fill=state)) + geom_col(position = "dodge") +  labs(x="object squashability", y="RT (ms)", title = "RT interaction of object state and squashability") + geom_errorbar(aes(ymin= (rawRTmean - SEM), ymax= (rawRTmean + SEM)), width=.25, position=position_dodge(width=0.9)) + theme_economist_white() + scale_fill_economist()

conditionMeansLOG %>% ggplot(aes(x=squashability, y=LogRTmean, fill=state)) + geom_col(position = "dodge") + labs(x="object squashability", y="log10(RT)", title = "log10(RT) interaction of object state and squashability") + geom_errorbar(aes(ymin= (LogRTmean - SEM), ymax=(LogRTmean + SEM)), width=.25, position=position_dodge(width=0.9))  + theme_economist_white() + scale_fill_economist()
